routes.description: Establish consciousness as the sole immediate ontological datum, reject nonconscious emergence as an explanation of experience, and show that a universal mental foundation can preserve objective structure, causal order, and scientific tractability.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if consciousness is shown to require no reduction to a nonexperiential substrate, while the proposed consciousness-first ontology accounts for observer-independent reality, differentiated subjects, regular causation, and nonspatiotemporal structure.

motionBridge.description: Connect the irreducibility of experience and the explanatory adequacy of universal subjectivity to the conclusion that consciousness is reality's ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: Show why descriptions of nonconscious physical quantities cannot entail experiential qualities and why positing strong emergence does not close that explanatory gap.
Explain how an external mental reality can remain observer-independent and appear as a stable physical world through perceptual representation and dissociative boundaries.
Ground causal power, differentiation, and natural regularities in the intrinsic dispositions and excitation modes of universal subjectivity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the constructed narrative self from consciousness itself so that rejecting a persistent personal agent does not eliminate experience.
Account for structure beyond fundamental spacetime through meaning-bearing cognitive or semantic relations.

routes.description: Separate rejection of materialist emergence from acceptance of idealism, develop a representation-based neutral monism, and require any consciousness-first ontology to explain structured order, boundaries, causal differentiation, and phenomenal character.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a neutral representational basis can accommodate phenomenal character without treating consciousness as universal substance, while idealism's mental-substrate designation leaves indispensable explanatory work unresolved.

motionBridge.description: Connect the sufficiency of neutral monism and the unresolved explanatory commitments of idealism to denial that consciousness must be reality's ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that rejecting matter-to-consciousness emergence does not by itself select analytic idealism over other nonmaterialist ontologies.
Locate phenomenal character in representations without requiring a separate physical organism, unified self, or universal conscious substance.
Require an account of how a designated mental substrate produces boundaries, predictive representations, structured order, and differentiated causal relations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether information integration supplies an explanatory connection to subjective experience rather than only an empirical correlation.
Use experiences lacking ordinary selfhood, space, or time to examine which features an adequate fundamental ontology must explain.

sections.title: Ontological Starting Point and the Emergence Gap
sections.rationale: This issue tests the principal inference from consciousness as an immediate datum and the explanatory gap of strong emergence to a consciousness-first ontology, including whether that inference excludes neutral alternatives.

sections.title: Objective Reality, Boundaries, and Natural Order
sections.rationale: A viable route must explain how observer-independent structure, perceptual representation, embodied boundaries, evolution, and stable causal regularities arise under its proposed ontology.

sections.title: Representation, Self-Models, and Phenomenal Character
sections.rationale: The dispute over whether phenomenal character belongs to representations, consciousness itself, or a persistent subject bears directly on whether neutral monism suffices or idealism is required.

sections.title: Integrated Information and Causal Existence
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether information integration merely predicts reports or supports claims about subjective viewpoints, self-existing complexes, and the location of causal power.

sections.title: Universal Subjectivity, Differentiation, and Nonspatiotemporal Structure
sections.rationale: The proposed universal subject must account for differentiated experiences and causal order without relying on a personal self, while also explaining structure when ordinary space and time are not fundamental.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Consciousness is the sole pre-theoretical given, so ontological parsimony favors reducing nature's complexity to consciousness rather than to a postulated nonexperiential substrate.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Bernardo by name, after which the uninterrupted first-person answer states his reductionist case.

response.rationale: This is a constructive opening that supplies the route's immediate-datum and parsimony premises rather than responding to an earlier opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly establishes the principal ontological starting point and clearly frames the proposed reduction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The parsimony claim and its consciousness-first conclusion are recoverable, though the conditions under which reduction is possible remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents idealism as the best account while using conditional language, but the parsimony premise alone only modestly supports that preference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is intelligible, but it leaves a material bridge from consciousness being epistemically given to consciousness being ontologically fundamental.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The support is principally a philosophical parsimony assertion; no developed comparison shows that a consciousness reduction is simpler overall.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion bridge by proposing consciousness as the sole basic ontological posit.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its positive starting point without materially interpreting or characterizing a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly calls consciousness the one pre-theoretical given and recommends reducing nature's complexity and variety to it.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Physical quantities do not entail experiential qualities, making strong emergence explanatorily empty; idealism is preferable if it can also preserve an objective, predictable world open to science.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer explicitly responds to the moderator's emergence alternative and continues in Kastrup's established speaking turn.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the explanatory-gap case and expressly conditions idealism's preference on preserving objectivity, prediction, and science.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it sharply identifies the central emergence requirement and acknowledges the principal adequacy condition on its alternative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between physical quantities and experiential qualities is clear, and the preference for idealism is explicitly conditional on explanatory adequacy.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is forceful about the emergence gap but expressly limits the idealist conclusion with multiple if-we-can-make-it-work conditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The quantities-to-qualities objection is coherent and the adequacy condition prevents a simple false dilemma, though idealism is not uniquely derived.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual mismatch supplies meaningful support, but the excerpt compresses the warrant that no physical description could entail experience.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the top of the central tier by directly stating both the emergence gap and the explanatory standard for idealism.

representationalCharity.rationale: Although physical emergence is rejected, the selected move does not develop a sufficiently specific strongest alternative for a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts physical parameters with qualities of experience and conditions idealism on explaining an external predictable world and science.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Rejecting matter-to-consciousness emergence does not establish analytic idealism, because the dissociation analogy still leaves the observed structure and order of the world unexplained.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the discussion to Susan, and the ensuing first-person critique directly names Bernardo and analytic idealism.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether rejecting physical emergence makes idealism preferable over other nonmaterialist accounts.

response.rationale: The move directly disputes the selection of analytic idealism after rejecting emergence and adds that dissociation still leaves worldly structure and order unexplained.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive selection inference and supplies an explanatory objection, though the rendered excerpt emphasizes the materialist problem more than the alternative comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The underdetermination objection is recoverable and stable, with only the range and comparative merits of alternative ontologies left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues that the earlier inference is insufficient rather than claiming to disprove idealism, which matches the support supplied.

charity.alternative: Idealism may be offered conditionally as the most economical account rather than as a deduction from the emergence gap alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: The conditional proposal must still explain why it outperforms neutral alternatives and accounts for observed structure.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between defeating materialist emergence and establishing idealism is valid and directly exposes an underdetermined inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual counterexample is strong, but the excerpt does not develop a representative neutral alternative or document the alleged residual failures.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central underdetermination bridge by denying that the emergence objection uniquely selects analytic idealism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves the possibility of idealism while correctly identifying the additional comparative and explanatory work still required.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked proposition and span reject the inference to analytic idealism and maintain that dissociation leaves objective structure and order unexplained.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Analytic idealism allows observer-independent external mental states that are not directly accessible but are represented through perception as the physical world.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo accepts the request to clarify his view and develops a sustained first-person account of analytic idealism.

components.text: The decisive demand is for idealism to preserve an observer-independent, structured external world rather than merely relabel experience.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the objectivity demand by distinguishing external mental states from their perceptual representation as a physical world, but it does not yet explain their structure.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer: it clearly contacts observer independence while leaving the demanded source of stable structure and order substantially unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: External mental states, indirect access, and perceptual representation are distinctly stated without material shifts in terminology or scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move states what analytic idealism allows rather than claiming the account has fully explained structure, so its force fits its conceptual aim.

charity.alternative: The prior objection asks for an explanation of external order, not merely permission to call inaccessible states mental.
charity.decisiveQualification: Observer independence answers one component but does not by itself explain structured regularity or why representations take their form.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The appearance-reality distinction is coherent and preserves externality, though mental-state structure is posited rather than derived.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The representational analogy supports compatibility with objectivity, but it offers little independent warrant for the external substrate being mental.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central objectivity bridge by explaining observer independence and perceptual access under analytic idealism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly addresses objectivity while its own formulation leaves visible the stronger explanatory demand concerning structured order.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the external world would remain without individual observers, consists of inaccessible mental states, and appears through perception.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Calling an inaccessible substrate mental adds no explanatory content unless the view accounts for the machinery, boundaries, and structured predictive representations through which the world appears.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker immediately challenges the preceding explanation in second person and invokes Blackmore's own interest in predictive processing.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether labeling the inaccessible represented substrate mental explains the machinery and origins of predictive representation.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges the explanatory content of the mental designation and asks where representations, predictive machinery, and their substrate come from.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the central explanatory inference and isolates the missing machinery, substrate, and representational-origin components.

precisionFindings.rationale: The demand is precisely framed as an explanatory challenge and consistently distinguishes representations, machinery, boundaries, and substrate.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker explicitly presents uncertainty and requests an account, fitting the interrogative force and avoiding a stronger unsupported refutation.

charity.alternative: The preceding account aims to establish compatibility between idealism and observer-independent representation, not a complete predictive-processing mechanism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Compatibility alone does not answer where representations, boundaries, and predictive organization originate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between redescribing a substrate and explaining representational machinery is explicit, consistent, and directly supports the requested consequence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The predictive-processing example specifies the missing explanandum, though the move does not establish that no idealist mechanism could supply it.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is a direct and highly specific statement of the central explanatory-demand bridge for the con route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge allows the limited compatibility result while accurately pressing the further explanatory burden that the route must satisfy.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks why brains are prediction machines, how calling everything mental helps, and where representations and their substrate originate.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Dissociative boundaries can appear as embodied sensory interfaces, while natural selection and stable non-deliberative dispositions account for biological differentiation, causal regularity, and physical predictability.
moves.attributionBasis: The response identifies bodily surfaces as dissociative boundaries and continues Kastrup's characteristic analytic-idealist explanation without a speaker change.

components.text: The decisive demand is for an account of representational boundaries, biological differentiation, and stable natural organization under idealism.
The earlier objection also demands an account of the world's observed structure and order rather than a dissociation label alone.

response.rationale: The reply identifies bodily sensory surfaces as dissociative boundaries and invokes reproduction, natural selection, and stable dispositions to address differentiation and regularity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive demand across several components, but the transition from possible dissociation to specific stable laws and representations remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The principal account is recoverable, but the move ranges from bodily boundaries to evolution and all natural regularity without fully marking scope transitions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The language presents a possible natural history and rejects ultimate why-questions, appropriately limiting the force of the speculative account.

charity.alternative: The objection seeks constitutive machinery and structured representation, not merely a historical story about how dissociative organisms reproduced.
charity.decisiveQualification: Evolution can explain selection after replicators exist but does not alone explain the origin or mechanics of dissociative boundaries.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evolutionary sequence is intelligible, but it relies on an unsupported conditional from possible dissociation to reproducible bounded organisms.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Skin, retina, and natural selection provide concrete illustrations, yet the foundational dissociation event and stable dispositions are substantially asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the central objectivity bridge through boundaries and evolution, though the causal-order component remains less developed.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the legitimate evolutionary component but only partially preserves the stronger constitutive demand about machinery and boundaries.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies sensory bodily surfaces as boundaries and proposes a reproducible dissociative process subsequently shaped by natural selection.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Neutral monism can avoid the hard problem by locating what-it-is-like in a bat's representation rather than moving from experience to a separately presumed physical bat.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly states her own view, develops Nagel's bat example, and asks Bernardo for his response at the end.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether a nonmaterialist alternative can avoid the hard problem while accommodating phenomenal character.
The opening move also requires a reason that consciousness, rather than a neutral representational basis, is the sole parsimonious foundation.

response.rationale: The move offers neutral monism as a direct rival and locates what-it-is-like in the bat's representation, thereby contesting idealism's claimed necessity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the central emergence and uniqueness inference with a specific rival, though the rival's ontology and explanatory machinery remain sketchy.

precisionFindings.rationale: The rival proposal is recoverable, but representation shifts between an experiential bearer and a neutral ontological item without full definition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly describes the account as exploratory and does not claim it is established, matching the limited warrant supplied.

charity.alternative: Idealism can agree that phenomenal character is representational while treating every representation as a state of universal consciousness.
charity.decisiveQualification: The neutral proposal must explain why representations possess phenomenal character without silently presupposing consciousness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternative blocks a simple inference to idealism, but the bridge from representation to what-it-is-like remains materially underexplained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Nagel's bat example clarifies the proposal, yet it functions mainly as a conceptual redescription rather than evidence for neutral sufficiency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge by proposing a neutral-monist route intended to avoid both emergence and universal consciousness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents a genuine alternative without caricaturing idealism, but it does not fully address the idealist's presupposition objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects movement from experience to a presumed physical bat and proposes that phenomenal character belongs to the bat's representation.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: The enduring personal agent may be a representational self-model, but even an experienced illusion presupposes consciousness, so dissolving the self does not eliminate phenomenality.
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup addresses Blackmore's known view, accepts her self-model analysis, and contrasts its consequences under materialism and idealism.

components.text: The decisive inference is that dissolving the enduring personal self can remove the need for consciousness as the condition of experienced representations.

response.rationale: The reply accepts the representational self-model but diagnoses that even an illusion or delusion must be experienced, defeating any inference from no enduring self to no consciousness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the premise it accepts, the inference it rejects, and the consequence that experience remains presupposed despite self-model dissolution.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between the narrative self-model and consciousness is explicit and consistently maintained through the illusion argument.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stipulated existence of experienced illusions, the limited claim that experience is presupposed has matching logical force.

charity.alternative: The neutral proposal may reject a persistent self while retaining phenomenal representations, rather than denying all consciousness or experience.
charity.decisiveQualification: Retaining phenomenal representations concedes experience but does not by itself establish idealism or universal subjectivity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between self and experience is clear, and the presupposition inference is strong within the stated case of experienced illusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument has substantial conceptual force, but the further contrast with materialist illusionism is compressed and not independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the top of the subsidiary tier by directly supporting the route's self-model distinction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly handles the no-self claim but partly shifts the rival toward eliminativism and overextends the concession beyond phenomenality.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts a delusive self-model while emphasizing that illusions and delusions are still experienced and therefore require experiential space.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: If phenomenal character belongs to representations, fleeting models at multiple processing levels may each have something it is like to be them even when the organizing self-model dissolves.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker declines Kastrup's final inference and develops a first-person proposal grounded in predictive hierarchies, meditation, and self-model dissolution.

components.text: The decisive demand is to explain phenomenality after distinguishing consciousness from the limited organizing self-model.

response.rationale: The reply agrees that the self-model is only a small part of processing and proposes phenomenal character across many fleeting representational models.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the phenomenality issue with a positive account, though it does not answer why each representation has something it is like to be it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposal is clear, but model, representation, and processing level are not sharply distinguished, and the scope of phenomenality is exploratory.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames the account as a question and tentative representational panpsychism, appropriately matching its speculative support.

charity.alternative: The preceding argument only says experience survives loss of a self-model; it does not require one phenomenality-bearing entity for every processing model.
charity.decisiveQualification: The new proposal must justify phenomenal character at each representational level rather than infer it from processing multiplicity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposal is internally intelligible, but the key bridge from representational processing to phenomenality at every level remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Predictive hierarchies and meditation motivate the possibility, yet the phenomenality attribution is chiefly speculative and lacks a discriminating warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central representation bridge by locating phenomenal character in models independently of a unified self.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the distinction between self-model and experience while fairly extending the debate to multiple representations.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts the limited phenomenal self-model with extensive other processing and asks whether all such models have something it is like.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: On the invoked IIT account, a maximal complex can exclude states to maximize integration while the excluded integrated processes retain subjective viewpoints outside the narrative self.
moves.attributionBasis: Kastrup explicitly returns to his theoretical comfort zone and introduces IIT as support for Blackmore's immediately preceding proposal.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether excluded and non-narrative representational processes can possess their own subjective viewpoints.

response.rationale: The move invokes IIT's maximal-complex and exclusion account to support subjective viewpoints outside the egoic self-model, directly addressing the proposed multiplicity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the multiple-viewpoint proposal with a named mechanism, although it relies on IIT rather than independently resolving phenomenality.

precisionFindings.rationale: Maximal complexes, exclusion, and retained viewpoints are stated consistently, though the conditions for excluded processes to remain integrated are implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents IIT's controversial subjective-viewpoint implication with more confidence than the excerpt's compressed theoretical support warrants.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The exclusion account is coherent at a schematic level, but the inference from retained integration to an independent subjective viewpoint is underexplained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A named theory supplies structure, yet no empirical or conceptual warrant is given for treating excluded complexes as phenomenal subjects.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly contacts the subsidiary integration bridge by connecting maximal integration and exclusion to subjective viewpoints.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply mainly endorses and theoretically supplements the preceding proposal rather than contesting a live alternative interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies the ego with a maximal IIT complex and claims that shed-off integrated processes retain subjective points of view.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Integrated information theory does not explain why greater information integration entails subjective experience or what it means for consciousness to exist in greater or lesser degree.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly addresses Bernardo and explicitly challenges his preceding account of integrated information theory.

components.text: The decisive demand is why integrated information entails phenomenality and what greater or lesser consciousness means.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the unexplained inference from information integration to subjective experience and requests clarification of graded consciousness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly isolates the decisive explanatory bridge and identifies the unclear consequence of interpreting the measure as degrees of consciousness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge consistently distinguishes measured integration, subjective experience, and the claim of more or less consciousness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker openly acknowledges limited understanding and asks for the missing explanation rather than asserting that IIT is false.

charity.alternative: IIT may be offered as an empirically predictive bridge or identity claim rather than a reductive derivation of phenomenality.
charity.decisiveQualification: Predictive mapping still does not explain or justify the asserted link between integration and what-it-is-like.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objection precisely separates correlation or measurement from explanation and states the missing inference without internal tension.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The theory's own integration-to-consciousness claim supplies a specific target, though the excerpt does not survey IIT's formal identity arguments.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the top of the subsidiary tier by directly testing whether integration explains subjective experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge allows IIT's operational value while accurately preserving the deeper explanatory question about subjective experience.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks why greater integrated information means more consciousness and why there is anything it is like to be the integrated system.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: IIT's deeper causal account leans toward idealism insofar as self-existing experiential complexes, rather than merely represented objects, possess causal structure and power.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo continues his answer by explicitly shifting from IIT's operational role to its limited ontological implications.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether IIT supplies more than an empirical mapping and what ontological conclusion its causal structure supports.

response.rationale: The reply concedes IIT is a predictive bridge, then argues cautiously that self-existing causal complexes lean toward rather than imply idealism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the ontological component and acknowledges the explanatory limitation, but it does not answer why integration entails phenomenality or degree.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited conclusion is clear, though technical phrases such as minimum complex and ontological dust are not explained in the selected evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly says IIT only leans toward and does not imply idealism, matching the limited causal-existence warrant.

charity.alternative: The objection asks for the phenomenality link, while IIT's causal-existence machinery may instead offer prediction and ontological constraints.
charity.decisiveQualification: Ontological constraints on causal complexes do not themselves explain why integration has subjective character.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The modest inference from self-existence to an idealist leaning is coherent, but its dependence on causal structure requires one implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move cites specific IIT commitments but compresses their meaning and offers no developed comparison with neutral or physical interpretations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It substantially contacts the subsidiary integration bridge while limiting IIT's role to prediction and a qualified ontological leaning.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly concedes the distinction and limits its conclusion, although it leaves the original phenomenality demand unanswered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls IIT a predictive mapping, then says causal structure depends on things existing for themselves and therefore only leans idealist.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Treating a dreaming subject as the cause of an imagined object is problematic when the causal first-person self invoked by that account lacks clear or stable existence.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan explicitly picks up Bernardo's dream example and interrogates the identity of the purported causal subject.

components.text: The decisive demand is to identify the self-existing causal subject when the account says a dreamer causes an imagined object.
The earlier concession that personal selves are representational creates a tension with treating an ordinary first-person self as causal.

response.rationale: The move directly identifies a tension between rejecting a stable personal self and invoking an I as the causal source of dream contents.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the causal-subject premise and states the consequence that the dream analogy lacks a clearly identified causal bearer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between the dream elephant, the asserted causal I, and the disputed enduring self is clear and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asks for clarification and identifies a prima facie tension without claiming that no idealist answer is possible.

charity.alternative: The causal subject could be consciousness or a broader experiential field rather than the narrative personal self represented within the dream.
charity.decisiveQualification: The account must explicitly distinguish that causal bearer from the self-model and explain how it differentiates particular dream events.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The tension is clearly formulated: an unstable representational self cannot be invoked without clarification as the stable causal source.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The shared concession about self-models gives the objection firm dialectical support, though it does not exclude a nonpersonal causal subject.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the explanatory-demand bridge by requiring identification and differentiation of causal agency under idealism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge fairly leaves room for a nonpersonal subject while requiring the missing distinction and causal specification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks what the causal 'you' is after both speakers acknowledged problems with treating the self as it ordinarily appears.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Particular experiences are excitations or behaviors of a single core subjectivity, rather than contents produced by separate individual material subjects.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo answers Susan's causal question, marks the transition to his own philosophy, and states his universal-subjectivity view.

components.text: The decisive demand is to identify a causal bearer of experience that is not the unstable narrative personal self.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes particular experiences from the single core subjectivity to which they are given, replacing the personal dream ego as bearer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies a nonpersonal subject and contacts the causal-bearer problem, though it does not yet explain differentiated causal production.

precisionFindings.rationale: The excitation-versus-core-subject distinction is stable, but the move leaves implicit how a single subject individuates particular experiences.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that experiences require one underlying dative subject exceeds what the metaphors alone establish, despite being coherently stated.

charity.alternative: Experiences may occur without a further subject behind them, with the subject constituted by patterns or representations themselves.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move needs an argument that the dative of experience is a distinct universal subject rather than a grammatical or conceptual projection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The bearer-content distinction is intelligible, but the inference from experiences being given to a single universal core subject remains a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dancer, top, river, and ripple metaphors illustrate the view but provide limited independent warrant for universal subjectivity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion bridge by identifying universal subjectivity as the proposed ontological foundation beneath particular experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges the no-personal-self concern but gives limited treatment to the strongest subjectless or process-based alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes particular excitations from the dative of experience and describes a core subject behind experiential contents.

moves.speaker: Susan Blackmore
moves.proposition: Ordinary dreams without an experienced self leave idealism and integrated-information accounts without a clear explanation of what causes one dream element rather than another.
moves.attributionBasis: Susan resumes the dream example and explicitly asks both IIT and analytic idealism to locate the relevant causal factors.

components.text: The decisive demand is how a universal nonpersonal subject differentiates and causes one particular dream element rather than another.
The move also asks whether IIT identifies the particular causal factors operative in an ordinary selfless dream.

response.rationale: The reply accepts that ordinary dreams can lack an experienced self and presses both idealism and IIT for a mechanism of particular causal differentiation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the unresolved differentiation problem and applies it to both recently offered causal frameworks through a concrete case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ordinary nonlucid-dream case and the demand for specific causal factors are clearly and consistently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker requests an explanation rather than concluding that either framework is impossible, exactly matching the warrant supplied.

charity.alternative: A universal subject need not appear as a self within the dream to be the underlying bearer or causal field of its contents.
charity.decisiveQualification: Identifying an underlying bearer still leaves unexplained why its intrinsic activity yields one differentiated content rather than another.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is clear: removing the experienced self leaves a specific unanswered question about what differentiates causal contributions within the dream.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The familiar possibility of selfless ordinary dreaming supplies a concrete test case, though the move does not independently establish its frequency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central explanatory-demand bridge by testing differentiation and causal specificity in a nonpersonal experiential field.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge grants the possible nonpersonal bearer and accurately focuses on the stronger unresolved issue of causal differentiation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes an ordinary dream lacking a salient self and asks what causal factors IIT or idealism assigns to its particular contents.

moves.speaker: Bernardo Kastrup
moves.proposition: Causal differentiation and complex natural order arise from the intrinsic properties, characteristic excitation modes, harmonics, and self-interference of the one universal field of subjectivity.
moves.attributionBasis: Bernardo directly answers the causality question by laying out analytic idealism's single-field ontology and its intrinsic properties.

components.text: The decisive demand is how one universal subject yields differentiated events and complex causal order without a personal agent.

response.rationale: The reply attributes differentiation to intrinsic properties, characteristic modes, harmonics, and self-interference of a universal field, directly proposing a mechanism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts causal differentiation with several mechanism-like constraints, though their application to particular dream contents remains schematic.

precisionFindings.rationale: The field-and-excitation account is recoverable, but the move shifts from illustrative wave behavior to the full complexity of nature without an explicit scope limit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The simple-rule analogy makes complex order plausible, but it does not fully warrant the stronger claim that universal subjectivity has the required intrinsic modes.

charity.alternative: The challenge requests discriminatory causal rules, and generic intrinsic properties could merely rename the regularities that require explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The account must specify constraints capable of selecting particular outcomes rather than only assert that characteristic modes exist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Field modes and interference can coherently generate complexity, but their transfer from physical waves to universal subjectivity requires a material analogy bridge.
